text: what's the idea behind "pure files"? why do we even recognise them as a concept? it doesn't sound as a common idea. isn't it over-complication? I may miss something.
node src/cli.ts show werk-test-scope 2>&1 | head -60; node src/cli.ts show werk-test-pure-list 2>&1 | head -40

card werk-test-scope  [decided]
Pure code gets a coverage number. I/O code gets a sampled behaviour list.
why: Generalized from werk's own split, so any project on this platform classifies its own modules the same way — werk is the first project built here, not the only one #product plans for. #werk-test-scope:src0 holds werk's own numbers as evidence, not as the rule.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

A rule for any module in any project on this platform, not only werk's four files today.

**1. Classify the module by one question.** Does a wrong line throw, hang, or crash — or does it quietly produce a result that looks correct? A quiet wrong answer is pure. A loud failure is I/O.

**2. Pure code gets a number.** A pure module is a plain function of its input, cheap to call from a test, and a bug in it never announces itself. Set a high line-coverage threshold. Testing it is cheap and missing a bug in it is expensive, so a hard number belongs here.

**3. I/O code gets a named list, never a percentage.** An I/O module holds something live — a child process, a socket, an open file, a network call. Covering a line here means faking the live thing, and a percentage rewards the fake, not the real risk. Write one list per module instead: named behaviours, no number.

**4. Find the behaviours by sampling, not by guessing.** Run several independent readings of the module against one brief: name what breaks the tool if this is wrong. Where the readings agree, that is the list. Where they disagree, the disagreement is a fact question about the code, not a taste question — read the source and settle it. Do not ask a person to guess at what code already does.

**5. Write each behaviour as a responsibility, not as a location.** 'A crash never loses the in-flight message' survives a rewrite. 'agent.ts line 326 throws' does not. A list built this way stays true when the file under it changes, as long as the module's job stays the same. Only a changed responsibility needs the list re-run — not a renamed file or a moved line.

card werk-test-pure-list  [decided]
The coverage check judges each pure file on its own, and a pure file with no test fails
why: A single percentage over the whole project mixes pure and I/O lines, so well-tested I/O code can hide an untested pure file. And a file that no test loads is missing from the coverage report, so a check that reads only the report never sees it and lets it pass.
subtree: 2 cards, 2 decided

Only pure code gets a coverage number (#werk-test-scope). The check therefore works from an explicit list of the pure files in the project, not from every file the report happens to contain.

**Each file on its own.** The coverage run writes a report with one entry per file that a test loaded. The check reads the report and compares

The idea is common, under another name. A "pure function" returns a result that depends only on its input. It does not read files, open sockets, or start processes. Gary Bernhardt's "functional core, imperative shell" pattern uses the same split. A "pure file" on this card means a file that holds only that kind of code.

**Why the map uses the split (#werk-test-scope):**

1. **A pure file gets a coverage number.** A test calls the function and checks the result. That is cheap. A bug in pure code gives a wrong result that looks correct, so only a test catches it. A high coverage number is fair here.
2. **An I/O file gets a list of named behaviours.** To cover a line in a file that runs a child process or a socket, the test must fake the process or the socket. Then the coverage number measures the fake, not the real risk.
3. **Without the split, you get one number for the whole project.** Well-tested I/O code can then hide a pure file that has no tests. #werk-test-pure-list exists to stop that.

**Where you are right:** the cost is in the parts that keep the list correct, not in the idea. This card needs an explicit list of pure files. #werk-test-pure-list-union needs a merge rule for that list. #werk-reflink-own-test-coverage adds a third rule. That is three cards to keep one list correct.

**A simpler option:** reverse the list. The check finds every source file by itself and treats each one as pure. A short list names the I/O files to skip. Then a forgotten entry makes the check stricter, not weaker. A new file is checked from its first commit with no extra step. The merge rule might then become unnecessary.

Next: should I propose this reversed list as an option on #werk-test-pure-list?
